title: Camels' Cousins: Llamas and Alpacas
summary: How llamas and alpacas are related to camels, how they are suited to life high in the Andes, and how people have used them for thousands of years.
poll: Llamas and alpacas are more useful to people than camels are.

versions.title: Camels Have Cousins
versions.text:
You know the camel. It has two cousins. They live far away. One is the llama. One is the alpaca.

They live in the Andes. These are high mountains. They are in South America. The air is thin up there. But their blood gets the air it needs.

Long ago, their kin lived in North America. Some went west. They grew to be camels. Some went south. They grew to be two wild kinds.

Then, 6,000 years ago, folks tamed the wild ones. The big kind gave us the llama. The small kind gave us the alpaca.

Both live in a herd. Both have long necks. Not one has a hump. Their feet have soft pads. Each foot has two toes. They chew food. Then they chew it once more.

The llama is big. It is strong. It can take a load. It goes up steep paths. The alpaca is small. Its thick coat is a soft fleece. It makes warm hats.

Both of them spit! Most of the time, they spit at each other.

In 1998, a team in Dubai did a test. A camel and a wild cousin had a calf. It was half camel. They named it Rama.

versions.title: Llamas and Alpacas: The Camel's Cousins
versions.text:
Most people in Saudi Arabia know the camel well. Fewer know that it has cousins on the other side of the world. They are the llama and the alpaca.

These animals live in the Andes, a long chain of mountains in South America. At such a high altitude, the air is thin and holds less oxygen. However, their blood is very good at picking up the oxygen they need.

Millions of years ago, the ancestors of the whole camel family lived in North America. Some of them crossed into Asia. Slowly, they became the camels we know today. Others traveled south and became two wild kinds, the guanaco and the vicuña.

About 6,000 years ago, people in the Andes domesticated these wild animals. Llamas came from the larger guanaco. Alpacas came from the smaller vicuña.

Both animals live in a herd. Both have long necks but no hump. Their feet have two toes and soft pads that do not harm the ground. Like camels, they chew their food, bring it back up, and chew it again.

The llama is much larger. It can carry a load of about a quarter of its own weight up steep paths. The alpaca is small. People raise it for its fiber, a soft fleece that comes in many natural colors.

Both animals can spit, but they usually spit at each other, not at people.

In 1998, scientists in Dubai tried an unusual test. A camel and a guanaco had a baby that was half camel. They named it Rama.

versions.title: Llamas and Alpacas: The Camel's Distant Cousins
versions.text:
Most people in Saudi Arabia know the camel well, but fewer people realize that it has two relatives living on the opposite side of the world: the llama and the alpaca. Together with camels, they belong to a family of animals called camelids.

Llamas and alpacas live in the Andes, an enormous chain of mountains running along western South America. At such a high altitude, the air is thin and contains noticeably less oxygen, yet their blood is especially efficient at collecting the oxygen their bodies require.

Millions of years ago, the ancestors of every camelid lived in North America. Some of them crossed into Asia, where they gradually developed into the camels we recognize today. Others traveled south and became two wild species, the guanaco and the vicuña.

About 6,000 years ago, people in the Andes began the domestication of these wild animals. Llamas were developed from the larger guanaco, while alpacas were developed from the smaller, more delicate vicuña.

Both animals live in herds, and both have long necks but no hump. Their feet have two toes and soft pads, which do not damage the ground the way hard hooves can. Like camels, they chew their food, bring it back up, and chew it a second time.

The llama is considerably larger and can carry a load of about a quarter of its own weight along steep mountain paths. For centuries before modern roads existed, the Inca people depended on long lines of llamas to move goods across their mountain empire. The alpaca is smaller, and people raise it mainly for its fiber, an extremely soft fleece that comes in many natural colors and helps insulate the animal against freezing nights.

Telling the two animals apart is easier than it might seem. A llama, which can weigh close to 200 kilograms, has long ears that curve like bananas, whereas an alpaca usually weighs less than 90 kilograms and has short, pointed ears.

Both animals can spit, although they usually spit at each other during arguments over food rather than at people.

In 1998, scientists in Dubai attempted an unusual experiment. A camel and a guanaco produced a hybrid baby that was half camel, and the scientists named it Rama.

versions.text:
Most people in Saudi Arabia are familiar with the camel, but considerably fewer realize that it has two relatives living on the opposite side of the world: the llama and the alpaca. Together with camels, these animals belong to a family of mammals that biologists classify as camelids.

Llamas and alpacas inhabit the Andes, an enormous chain of mountains extending along the entirety of western South America, where the atmosphere at such high altitude is thin and contains considerably less oxygen; nevertheless, their blood is remarkably efficient at collecting whatever oxygen their bodies require.

Millions of years ago, the ancestors of every camelid lived in North America. Some of them eventually crossed into Asia, where they gradually developed into the camels we recognize today, while others migrated south and evolved into two distinct wild species, the guanaco and the vicuña.

Approximately 6,000 years ago, communities in the high Andes began domesticating these wild animals, developing llamas from the considerably larger guanaco and alpacas from the smaller, considerably more delicate vicuña.

Both animals live in herds, and both possess elegant long necks but no hump whatsoever. Their feet have two toes and cushioned pads, which do not damage the fragile mountain vegetation the way hard hooves can, and like camels, they chew their food, regurgitate it, and chew it a second time.

The llama is considerably larger and can carry a load equivalent to roughly a quarter of its own body weight along steep mountain trails, which explains why, for centuries before modern highways existed, the Inca civilization depended on long caravans of llamas to transport goods across its mountainous empire. The alpaca is comparatively smaller, and communities raise it primarily for its fiber, an extremely soft fleece that comes in numerous natural colors and helps insulate the animal against freezing nighttime temperatures.

versions.title: Llamas and Alpacas: The Camel's Distant Cousins
versions.text:
Most people throughout Saudi Arabia are intimately familiar with the camel, yet comparatively few realize that it possesses two genuinely distant relatives living on the opposite side of the entire world: the llama and the alpaca. Together with camels, these three kinds of animals belong to a broader family of mammals that biologists formally classify under the collective term camelids.

Llamas and alpacas inhabit the Andes, an immense mountain chain extending continuously along the entirety of western South America, where the surrounding atmosphere at such extraordinary altitude is notably thin and contains considerably less available oxygen than air found at sea level; nevertheless, their highly specialized blood remains remarkably efficient at collecting whatever oxygen their bodies urgently and continuously require to function at such heights.

Millions of years ago, the common ancestors of every existing camelid species inhabited North America exclusively. Some of these ancestral populations eventually migrated across into Asia, where they gradually evolved over countless generations into the camels we readily recognize today, while others instead journeyed southward and evolved into two entirely distinct wild species, namely the guanaco and the considerably smaller vicuña.

Approximately 6,000 years ago, human communities inhabiting the Andes initiated the gradual domestication of these wild animals, developing llamas specifically from the considerably larger guanaco and alpacas instead from the smaller, more delicate vicuña.

Both animals characteristically live together in herds, and both possess elegant, considerably elongated necks while entirely lacking any hump whatsoever. Their feet are equipped with two toes and soft cushioned pads, which, unlike hard hooves, do not damage the fragile mountain vegetation underfoot as they move, and like camels, they chew their food, regurgitate it, and subsequently chew it a second time in a repeated digestive process known as rumination.

The llama is considerably larger overall and can carry a substantial load approximating a quarter of its own body weight along steep, treacherous mountain trails, which explains precisely why, for centuries before modern highways ever existed in that region, the Inca civilization depended extensively and continuously on long caravans of llamas to transport goods across its vast, mountainous empire. The alpaca, by distinct contrast, is considerably smaller, and communities raise it primarily for its fiber, an extraordinarily soft fleece available in numerous natural colors that helps insulate the animal quite effectively against the freezing nighttime temperatures common at high altitude.

Distinguishing reliably between the two animals proves considerably easier than one might initially suppose. A llama, which can weigh close to 200 kilograms when fully grown, possesses elongated ears that curve gracefully like bananas, whereas an alpaca typically weighs less than 90 kilograms and instead has short, pointed ears that stand upright.

Both animals are entirely capable of spitting when provoked, although they usually direct this particular behavior at each other during disagreements over food rather than at any human observers who happen to be nearby.

In 1998, scientists conducting research in Dubai attempted a genuinely unusual experiment in which a camel and a guanaco successfully produced a hybrid offspring that was genetically half camel and half guanaco, and the researchers subsequently named this remarkable, unprecedented animal Rama, in recognition of the experiment's scientific significance.

From the oxygen-rich blood that allows them to thrive on windswept Andean peaks to the soft, two-toed feet that spare fragile mountain ground, every camelid characteristic examined here, whether found in a desert camel or a highland llama, ultimately traces back to the same shared ancestry that first diverged in North America many millions of years ago.

MID.modelAnswer: Llamas and alpacas are well suited to life high in the Andes because their blood is especially good at collecting oxygen, which helps them survive where the altitude is so high that the air has less oxygen than usual. Their soft, padded feet also help, since the two-toed pads do not damage the steep mountain ground the way a hard hoof would. People domesticated these animals from wild ancestors thousands of years ago, and they still live together in a herd today, and the alpaca's soft fiber, or fleece, is especially prized by the people who raise it in those mountain herds.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the history of the camelid family helps us understand why llamas and camels are alike in some ways and different in others. Support your answer with evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained at least one similarity and one difference.
I connected these to where the ancestors moved and how they adapted.

HIGH.modelAnswer: The history of the camelid family explains both the similarities and the differences between llamas and camels, because all of them descended from common ancestors that once lived in North America millions of years ago. Some of those ancestors crossed into Asia and became camels, while others moved south into the high-altitude Andes and became the wild guanaco and vicuña, which people later brought through domestication to create the llama and alpaca we know today. Because they share the same camelid ancestry, llamas and camels are alike in basic ways, such as chewing their food a second time and living in herds, but millions of years spent in very different environments gave them different features, like the camel's hump for desert travel. The 1998 hybrid named Rama, born from a camel and a guanaco, is further evidence of just how closely related these animals still are beneath their differences.
